sections.title: Red Flags: Contact Lens Wear
content: Pseudomonas Aeruginosa keratitis (rapid onset)
Acanthamoeba keratitis (pain out of proportion to exam)
Corneal neovascularization due to hypoxia
Acute red eye (CLARE/CLPU)
Tight lens syndrome

sections.title: Management of Complications
content: Step 1: Immediate cessation of lens wear
Step 2: Culture of lens case and ocular surface if infection suspected
Step 3: Topical antibiotics (Fluoroquinolones) for suspected MK
Step 4: Lubrication and mast cell stabilizers for GPC
Step 5: Refit lens geometry or material after resolution

content.explanation: E: Epithelial microcysts, D: Descemet's striae, E: Endothelial polymegethism, M: Myopic shift, A: Acute endothelial cell loss.

sections.title: Fitting Principles for Keratoconus
content: Aim for 'Three-point touch' in corneal RGP fitting: central apical touch and mid-peripheral bearing.
Scleral lenses vault the entire cornea and limbus, landing on the conjunctiva, eliminating corneal mechanical stress.
Piggyback: Place a thin high-Dk silicone hydrogel lens under the RGP to enhance comfort.
Calculate 'Vault' for scleral lenses: Ensure 100-200 microns of clearance after settling.
Topography-guided fitting is standard: Use E-map or Sagittal maps to predict base curve.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Never dispense CLs to a patient with active blepharitis or MGD without prior treatment.
Always check oxygen transmissibility (Dk/t) for patients with history of hypoxic stress.
For scleral lenses, use preservative-free saline to prevent toxic epitheliopathy.
Hydrogel lenses are contraindicated in patients with extreme dry eye; recommend daily disposables with high water content or silicone hydrogel with low modulus.
In Keratoconus, regular topography is essential to monitor progression before fitting.
